title: The minimally invasive interbody selection algorithm for spinal deformity
article_subtype: Retrospective analysis and Delphi consensus algorithm development
condition_or_topic: Selection of minimally invasive interbody approaches for adult spinal deformity (ASD).
clinical_background: ASD can involve coronal or sagittal deformity alongside degenerative disease and can substantially impair well-being, particularly in older adults. Nonoperative care generally does not improve patient-reported outcomes, while surgery can reduce pain and disability; complex open procedures in elderly patients have reported complication rates as high as 80%. Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) uses interbody grafts for fusion, indirect decompression, and alignment correction with potentially less morbidity, but criteria for choosing an interbody approach at each spinal level are lacking.
objectives: Develop the minimally invasive interbody selection algorithm (MIISA) as a decision-making framework for choosing an interbody approach in MIS for deformity.
Describe approach selection and the segmental lordosis correction achieved by each approach at the treated lumbar levels.
Compare preoperative and minimum 2-year postoperative radiographic parameters and clinical outcomes.
clinical_question: In adults with ASD undergoing circumferential MIS, how do ALIF, ACR, LLIF, and TLIF compare in segmental lordosis correction at each treated lumbar level, and how do radiographic parameters and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) change from before surgery to minimum 2-year follow-up?
study_design: Multicenter retrospective analysis of a database of circumferential minimally invasive surgery (cMIS) for adult spinal deformity, combined with a Delphi process. During multiple meetings over a 3-month period, 11 surgeons used surveys and the database findings to reach consensus on the minimally invasive interbody selection algorithm (MIISA).

population.description: Adults with spinal deformity who underwent cMIS with interbody graft placement and percutaneous segmental pedicle screw instrumentation between 2015 and 2018. The analysis included 100 patients and 338 interbody grafts.
inclusion_criteria: A minimum of 2 years of postoperative radiographic follow-up.
exclusion_criteria: Interbody graft placement accompanied by open posterior pedicle screw fixation, including open or hybrid surgery.
Revision surgery in a previously instrumented spine.

interventions: cMIS using anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF).
cMIS using lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF), including the transpsoas approach.
cMIS using LLIF with anterior column release (ACR) and division of the anterior longitudinal ligament.
cMIS using transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF).
comparators: ALIF, LLIF, LLIF with ACR, and TLIF were compared by treated lumbar level for interbody approach selection and segmental lordosis.

primary: Surgeons’ interbody approach preferences by lumbar level and surgical goal.
Change in segmental lordosis by treated level and interbody approach.
secondary: Preoperative and postoperative Oswestry Disability Index (ODI).
Preoperative and postoperative sagittal vertical axis (SVA), pelvic incidence (PI), pelvic tilt (PT), lumbar lordosis (LL), PI-LL mismatch, and coronal Cobb angle.

statistical_methods: Analyses used IBM SPSS software (version 25, IBM Corp.). ANOVA assessed differences among interbody fusion groups, with post hoc Bonferroni correction for comparisons involving more than two groups. The significance threshold was an alpha level of 0.05.
follow_up: Minimum postoperative radiographic follow-up of 2 years; mean follow-up 39.3 months (range 24–74 months).
interpretation: Among 100 patients with predominantly moderate adult spinal deformity treated with 338 interbody devices, the authors observed significant improvement at 2-year follow-up in PI-LL mismatch, coronal Cobb angle, and ODI. LLIF was the most frequently selected approach from L1 to L4; surgeons also used TLIF and ALIF at L4–5, while TLIF was most common at L5–S1. ACR produced the greatest segmental lordosis gains at L2–3 and L3–4, and ALIF did so at L4–5 and L5–S1. Approach choice did not significantly affect lordosis at L1–2. At L4–5, the lordosis gains with LLIF and ACR did not differ significantly; the authors suggest that the small ACR group (n = 4) may partly explain its lower observed change. TLIF provided little lordosis restoration at L4–5 and L5–S1 in this cohort. The authors consider the MIISA a framework for selecting an interbody approach, rather than a substitute for individualized surgical decisions.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors describe their approach-specific lordosis results as broadly consistent with earlier reports, although the 4°–10° gains observed with ACR in their cMIS cohort were lower than expected from previous studies. Published ALIF studies reported segmental gains of 5.4° to 15°, depending on level. Alvi et al. reported mean gains of 2.1° with static cages and 5.0° with expandable cages in MIS TLIF; Hawasli et al. reported 2.3° and 5.2°, respectively. Carlson et al. reported a weighted average gain of 2.1° and a trend toward greater postoperative lordosis when cages were placed closer to the anterior vertebral cortex. For LLIF without ACR, Xu et al. reported a mean gain of 5.6° in grade II spondylolisthesis, with 75% achieving complete reduction, whereas Miscusi et al. reported a 2.0° lordosis gain and 11.3° mean coronal Cobb angle correction. Turner et al. reported gains of 16.3° with ACR and 5.7° without it; another cited study reported an 11.8° mean gain with ACR. Prior reports found gains of 17.3°–18.7° when ACR was combined with Scoliosis Research Society–Schwab grades 1 or 2 posterior osteotomies, but also associated PCO with an almost 7-fold increase in subsidence rates. The authors note that Leveque et al. found ACR correction to average 54% of implanted cage lordosis. They also cite evidence that the relationship between segmental gains and regional LL differs by approach, while cautioning that global alignment changes make direct correlations difficult.
clinical_implications: In appropriately selected patients with moderate deformity, less invasive interbody treatment was associated with improved PI-LL mismatch, coronal Cobb angle, and ODI.
ACR at L2–3 and L3–4 may provide more segmental lordosis than TLIF and may help limit construct length; its approach corridor is often more favorable than that of ALIF.

L4–5 lateral approaches have been reported to cause temporary ipsilateral leg weakness and sensory symptoms related to psoas trauma and nerve stretch. Reported ACR complications can include catastrophic iliac vessel injury requiring immediate vascular intervention, although major vascular, visceral, and neurological complications have been reported as exceedingly rare (< 1%) when experienced surgeons perform the procedure.

The authors state that gains in segmental lordosis correlate with better patient-reported outcomes, while noting that direct and indirect neural decompression are major contributors and that the relationship with regional LL and PI-LL mismatch is complex.
practice_implications: Use the MIISA alongside careful patient selection, comorbidities, baseline radiographic findings, anatomical access constraints, and surgical goals; the authors suggest using MISDEF-2 with MIISA to help determine the overall MIS strategy.

For L1–4, the surgeons generally favored lateral approaches over TLIF and reserved ACR for patients needing the greatest segmental lordosis gain. L3–4 ALIF can be considered when ALIF is also used at L4–5 and L5–S1; MIS TLIF remains an option.

At L4–5, the surgeons' preference order was LLIF, TLIF, then ALIF. ALIF can be considered when disc-height and lordosis restoration are goals; LLIF with or without ACR also depends on the surgeon's expertise at this challenging level. In this cohort, TLIF did not demonstrate significant lordosis restoration there.

At L5–S1, the surgeons generally preferred ALIF when additional segmental lordosis was needed and TLIF when preoperative segmental lordosis was adequate. A lateral approach is generally infeasible at this level because of the iliac crest.

Consider the treated level, the relationship of the great vessels to the spine, and surgeon familiarity when deciding whether to use ACR. The apex of the scoliotic curve, neural compression, foraminal osteophytic hooks, and prior abdominal or retroperitoneal surgery also require consideration.
limitations: The retrospective design and review of data from a relatively small number of surgeons across multiple centers introduced variability in data collection that was difficult to control.
One nonsurgeon performed the radiographic measurements, so interrater agreement could not be calculated.
The analysis did not distinguish static, expandable, lordotic, and hyperlordotic cages, although cage choice and intraoperative anatomical constraints can affect achievable segmental lordosis.
Some patients received different interbody approaches at different levels, preventing attribution of pelvic-parameter or PI-LL mismatch changes to a single approach.
Approach groups were unequal, with LLIF used in 70% of cases; the lack of standardization may bias the reported mean segmental lordosis.

The MIISA does not capture every factor that can influence approach selection, including curve apex, the degree and location of neural compression, foraminal osteophytic hooks, vascular anatomy, and previous abdominal or retroperitoneal surgery.
open_questions: The authors state that direct relationships between changes in segmental lordosis, regional LL, and PI-LL mismatch are difficult to establish because non–index-level biomechanics and global sagittal alignment interact.
The frequency and outcomes of using lordotic rather than 0° interbody cages in MIS for ASD remain to be clarified.
future_directions: Study the frequency and outcomes of lordotic versus 0° interbody cages in MIS for ASD.
Conduct larger prospective studies and examine how the findings correlate with health-related quality-of-life measures.

main_conclusion: The authors present MIISA as a framework for selecting interbody approaches in cMIS for ASD, to be used alongside patient selection, anatomical constraints, baseline alignment, comorbidities, and surgical goals. Their surgeons favored lateral approaches at L1–4, reserving ACR for greater lordosis requirements; at L4–5 they most often selected LLIF, then TLIF and ALIF, although TLIF did not demonstrate significant lordosis restoration; at L5–S1 they favored ALIF when additional segmental lordosis was needed and TLIF when baseline lordosis was adequate.
narrative_summary:
The authors developed MIISA through a Delphi process involving 11 experienced surgeons, informed by a retrospective analysis of 100 cMIS procedures for ASD using 338 interbody devices. Patients had at least 2 years of postoperative radiographic follow-up. The analysis compared approach selection and segmental lordosis across lumbar levels, alongside clinical and regional alignment outcomes.

LLIF was the most frequently used approach from L1–2 through L4–5. At L2–3 and L3–4, ACR yielded segmental lordosis increases of 10.9° and 10.4°, respectively, greater than those reported with LLIF or TLIF (p < 0.001 at each level). At L4–5, ALIF produced a 9.2° increase, compared with 5.4° for LLIF, 4.6° for ACR, and 0.8° for TLIF (p < 0.001). At L5–S1, the increase was greater with ALIF than TLIF (5.3° vs 1.9°, p = 0.003). At minimum 2-year follow-up, PI-LL mismatch declined from 15.2° to 10.8° (p = 0.007), coronal Cobb angle from 22.9° to 10.0° (p < 0.00001), and ODI from 50.2 to 31.1 (p < 0.00001).

The authors position MIISA as guidance rather than a substitute for individual assessment. They note limitations from retrospective design, approach imbalance, heterogeneous procedures, and unmeasured differences among cage types.

notable_adverse_events: The article cites prior reports associating LLIF approaches at L4–5, with or without ACR, with temporary postoperative ipsilateral leg weakness and sensory symptoms attributed to psoas muscle trauma and nerve stretch; it gives no rate for these events in the study cohort.
The discussion cites prior reports of potentially catastrophic iliac vein or artery injury with ACR; it gives no rate for this specific injury in the study cohort.

Citing prior reports concerning ACR performed by experienced surgeons, the authors describe major vascular, visceral, and neurological complications as exceedingly rare (< 1%); this is not a complication rate measured in the study cohort.
The discussion cites prior reports associating PCO performed with ACR with an almost 7-fold increase in subsidence rates; this is not a comparison measured in the study cohort.

subgroup_analyses: By treated level, approach selection shifted from a predominance of LLIF at L1–2, L2–3, and L3–4 to greater use of TLIF and ALIF at L4–5; at L5–S1, only TLIF and ALIF were used. The level-specific counts and percentages are reported in main_findings.

By level and approach, the gain in segmental lordosis did not differ significantly at L1–2 (p = 0.445), was greatest with ACR at L2–3 and L3–4 (p < 0.001 at each level), was greatest with ALIF at L4–5 (p < 0.001 across approaches), and was greater with ALIF than TLIF at L5–S1 (p = 0.003). The corresponding approach-specific values are reported in main_findings.
secondary_results: At surgery, mean age was 64.7 years (range 48–83); the cohort included 71 (71) females and 29 (29) males. Mean BMI was 27.8 kg/m2 (range 16.8–45.4), mean preoperative ODI was 50.2, and mean follow-up was 39.3 months (range 24–74).
Mean SVA changed from 4.2 cm preoperatively to 3.8 cm at a minimum postoperative follow-up of 2 years; this difference was not significant (p = 0.854).
Mean PT was 23.6° both preoperatively and at a minimum postoperative follow-up of 2 years, without a significant difference (p = 0.786).

Mean PI was 53.1° preoperatively and 52.4° at a minimum postoperative follow-up of 2 years. The article provides no p value and notes that the values are within 1.5% standard of error for a static radiographic parameter.
Mean LL increased from 37.9° preoperatively to 41.6° at a minimum postoperative follow-up of 2 years (p = 0.002).
Mean PI-LL mismatch decreased from 15.2° preoperatively to 10.8° at a minimum postoperative follow-up of 2 years (p = 0.007).
Mean coronal Cobb angle decreased from 22.9° preoperatively to 10.0° at a minimum postoperative follow-up of 2 years (p < 0.00001).
Mean ODI decreased from 50.2 preoperatively to 31.1 at a minimum postoperative follow-up of 2 years (p < 0.00001); the narrative reports a postoperative reduction of 19 points.
The authors describe LLIF without ACR as generally not producing significant restoration of lordosis. They also report that TLIF at L4–5 did not demonstrate significant lordosis restoration.

document_sections.heading: OBJECTIVE
document_sections.content: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) for spinal deformity uses interbody procedures to correct alignment, decompress indirectly, and achieve arthrodesis. Criteria for selecting among these procedures were lacking. The authors developed the minimally invasive interbody selection algorithm (MIISA) as a decision-making framework for deformity surgery.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: The authors examined a retrospective, level-specific lumbar dataset of circumferential MIS (cMIS) for adult spinal deformity (ASD), collected over a 5-year period. They assessed surgeons’ approach choices and changes in segmental lordosis, then used those findings in a Delphi session to develop an algorithm leading to anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF), anterior column release (ACR), lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF), or transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF). They compared preoperative findings with radiographic and clinical outcomes at 2 years.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: Eleven surgeons performed 100 cMIS procedures for ASD, placing 338 interbody devices; follow-up lasted at least 2 years. Approach selection was recorded from L1 to S1, and development of MIISA achieved substantial agreement. LLIF was generally favored at L1–2 (91.7%), L2–3 (85.2%), and L3–4 (80.7%). ACR was used most often at L3–4 (8.4%) and L2–3 (6.2%). At L4–5, the commonly selected procedures were LLIF (69.5%), TLIF (15.9%), and ALIF (9.8%); at L5–S1, they were TLIF (61.4%) and ALIF (38.6%). Changes in segmental lordosis differed by approach. ALIF produced larger gains, particularly at L4–5 (9.2°) and L5–S1 (5.3°), while ACR produced substantial gains at L2–3 (10.9°) and L3–4 (10.4°). LLIF without ACR generally did not produce significant restoration of lordosis. At 2 years, lumbar lordosis (LL), pelvic incidence–LL mismatch, coronal Cobb angle, and Oswestry Disability Index had improved significantly.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: MIISA offers surgeons consistent guidance when planning MIS for deformity. At L1–4, this group favored lateral approaches over TLIF and used ACR when the greatest increase in segmental lordosis was needed. Their preference order at L4–5 was LLIF, TLIF, then ALIF, although TLIF did not demonstrate significant restoration of lordosis. At L5–S1, they generally chose ALIF when additional segmental lordosis was desired and TLIF when baseline segmental lordosis was sufficient.

document_sections.heading: The minimally invasive interbody selection algorithm for spinal deformity
document_sections.content: Adult spinal deformity (ASD) includes deformities in different planes, such as coronal scoliosis and sagittal deformity, and frequently accompanies substantial degenerative disease. It can markedly impair well-being across age groups, especially among older people. Nonoperative care generally does not improve patient-reported outcomes and, at best, maintains symptoms in a progressive condition. Surgery has been shown to reduce pain and disability, but open procedures can carry considerable morbidity; reported complication rates reach 80% for the most complex operations in elderly patients. Less invasive and MIS techniques have treated degenerative disease effectively with less morbidity. Their increasing application to ASD may allow more patients to undergo less invasive deformity surgery. Interbody selection is central to MIS for deformity because interbody grafts provide arthrodesis, indirect decompression, and segmental alignment correction; posterior pedicle screw–rod fixation usually accompanies them. Relative to conventional open surgery, these procedures may reduce posterior paraspinous muscle disruption, blood loss, and postoperative pain while improving health-related quality-of-life outcomes. Approach selection depends on patient anatomy, the surgeon’s familiarity with MIS, and the pathology being treated. Anatomical restrictions, particularly at L5–S1, do not eliminate variation in approach choice at each level. MIISA is proposed to guide those choices, supplemented by segmental correction values for each treated level.

document_sections.heading: Algorithm Design
document_sections.content: Over multiple meetings spanning 3 months, 11 surgeons experienced in minimally invasive deformity surgery developed MIISA through a Delphi process. Surveys addressed preferred approaches by level and, in subsequent rounds, whether surgery aimed to restore height, lordosis, or both. The algorithm underwent repeated revisions until consensus was reached. Its development drew on the MIS–International Spine Study Group database: 338 interbody grafts placed during 100 cMIS deformity operations performed between 2015 and 2018. These operations combined interbody treatment with percutaneous segmental pedicle screw instrumentation. Every patient had at least 2 years of postoperative radiographic follow-up. Grafts used with open posterior pedicle screw fixation, including open or hybrid operations, and revisions of previously instrumented spines were excluded. Participating centers obtained local IRB approval, and patients consented before database enrollment. The analysis examined demographics and procedure descriptions. Clinical assessment before surgery and at a postoperative minimum of 2 years used the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). An independent site measured sagittal vertical axis (SVA), pelvic incidence (PI), pelvic tilt (PT), lumbar lordosis (LL), PI-LL mismatch, coronal Cobb angle, and segmental lordosis on preoperative and postoperative upright, standing 36-inch long-cassette radiographs. Segmental lordosis represented sagittal correction at the treated level and was assessed by approach. The approaches were ALIF, LLIF including the transpsoas approach, LLIF with ACR involving section of the anterior longitudinal ligament, and TLIF. The Delphi process also asked surgeons why they selected each approach. The article illustrates the anterior, lateral, and posterior interbody approaches.

document_sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: The authors used IBM SPSS software (version 25, IBM Corp.) for all statistical analyses. ANOVA assessed differences between interbody fusion groups. Comparisons involving more than two groups received a post hoc Bonferroni correction. The threshold for statistical significance was an alpha level of 0.05.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: During a 5-year period, 11 surgeons performed 100 cMIS operations for ASD and placed 338 interbody devices. Mean age at surgery was 64.7 years, 71% of patients were female, mean BMI was 27.8 kg/m2, and mean preoperative ODI was 50.2. Postoperative follow-up lasted at least 2 years and averaged 39.3 months. The authors recorded approach choice at every level from L1 through S1 and compared changes in segmental lordosis. Preoperative segmental lordosis did not differ significantly among the four treatment groups at each level. A patient-demographics and clinical-characteristics table reports age and BMI ranges, sex counts, baseline ODI, and follow-up range.

document_sections.heading: Level-by-Level Analysis
document_sections.content: The level-specific analysis reports the number and proportion of each interbody approach used from L1–2 through L5–S1 and compares the resulting changes in segmental lordosis. The accompanying tables display approach selection by level and preoperative, postoperative, and change values for segmental lordosis, together with between-group p values.

document_sections.heading: L1–2
document_sections.content: At L1–2, MIS TLIF was performed in 2 patients (4.2%), MIS LLIF in 44 (91.7%), and MIS ACR in 2 (4.2%); no ALIF was performed. The change in segmental lordosis did not differ significantly by approach. Lordosis changed by 2.6° per level with TLIF, 3.8° with LLIF without ACR, and 7.4° with ACR. The authors considered the small ACR group a likely reason why its lordosis change did not reach a statistically significant between-approach difference.

document_sections.heading: L2–3
document_sections.content: At L2–3, 1 patient received ALIF (1.2%), 6 received MIS TLIF (7.4%), 69 received MIS LLIF (85.2%), and 5 received MIS ACR. The level-specific text gives the ACR proportion as 6.6%, whereas the approach-selection table and abstract give 6.2%. Segmental lordosis increased significantly more with ACR than with LLIF or TLIF: 10.9° vs 4.2° vs 1.4°, respectively (p < 0.001).

document_sections.heading: L3–4
document_sections.content: At L3–4, 2 patients underwent ALIF (2.4%), 7 underwent MIS TLIF (8.4%), 67 underwent MIS LLIF (80.7%), and 7 underwent MIS ACR (8.4%). The increase in segmental lordosis was significantly greater with ACR than with LLIF or TLIF: 10.4° vs 4.6° vs 2.1°, respectively (p < 0.001).

document_sections.heading: L4–5
document_sections.content: At L4–5, ALIF was used in 8 patients (9.8%), MIS TLIF in 13 (15.9%), MIS LLIF in 57 (69.5%), and MIS ACR in 4 (4.9%). ALIF yielded a significantly greater increase in segmental lordosis than LLIF, ACR, or TLIF: 9.2° vs 5.4° vs 4.6° vs 0.8°, respectively (p < 0.001). Restoration of segmental lordosis did not differ significantly between LLIF and ACR, but the increase with LLIF significantly exceeded that with TLIF (p < 0.001).

document_sections.heading: L5–S1
document_sections.content: At L5–S1, 17 patients underwent ALIF (38.6%) and 27 underwent MIS TLIF (61.4%); none underwent LLIF. ALIF produced a significantly greater gain in segmental lordosis than TLIF: 5.3° vs 1.9° (p = 0.003).

document_sections.heading: Global/Regional Radiographic and Clinical Analysis
document_sections.content: The analyzed patients generally had moderate deformities. Mean baseline SVA was 4.2 cm and mean baseline PT was 23.6°; neither changed significantly after surgery. Mean baseline PI-LL mismatch was 15.2° and mean baseline coronal Cobb angle was 22.9°. After surgery, PI-LL mismatch decreased significantly to 10.8° (p < 0.01), and coronal Cobb angle decreased significantly to 10° (p < 0.01). ODI fell significantly by 19 points (p < 0.00001). A table presents mean radiographic and clinical measurements before surgery and at a postoperative minimum of 2 years, with their p values.

document_sections.heading: The MIISA
document_sections.content: MIISA generally separates treated lumbar levels into L1–4, L4–5, and L5–S1. ALIF is unusual at L1–4, although L3–4 ALIF can be considered when ALIF is also used at L4–5 and L5–S1. At L1–4, preferred MIS options are usually LLIF with or without ACR; the choice depends on the surgeon’s familiarity with the procedure and the amount of segmental lordosis needed. MIS TLIF is another option at these levels. At L4–5, ALIF can be considered to restore disc height and encourage lordosis. LLIF and ACR can also restore segmental lordosis there, subject to the surgeon’s expertise at this challenging level. LLIF at L4–5, with or without ACR, has been reported to cause temporary postoperative weakness and sensory symptoms in the ipsilateral leg through psoas muscle trauma and nerve stretch; many surgeons in this group therefore chose TLIF. In these data, LLIF with or without ACR and TLIF restored less lordosis at L4–5 than ALIF. At L5–S1, obstruction by the iliac crest generally prevents a lateral approach. ALIF is an option when maximizing disc height and lordosis is the goal; MIS TLIF is an option when other goals take priority. The algorithm illustration specifies LLIF1 as prepsoas or transpsoas lateral interbody fusion when up to 5° of segmental lordosis is desired, noting that restoration of height between L1 and L4 is consistent but restoration of lordosis is not. It describes ACR2 for a desired segmental lordosis gain of ≥ 10° and TLIF3 as allowing direct decompression of foraminal or lateral recess stenosis.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors reviewed 100 patients treated by experienced minimally invasive deformity surgeons with 338 interbody devices. Deformities were predominantly moderate, characterized by mean SVA < 5 cm, PT < 25°, PI-LL mismatch of 15°, and coronal Cobb angle > 20°. At 2 years, PI-LL mismatch, coronal Cobb angle, and ODI-based clinical status had improved significantly. LLIF predominated between L1 and L4. At L4–5 it was less frequent; surgeons also used TLIF and ALIF because lateral access can be difficult and TLIF can provide direct decompression. MIS TLIF was most frequent at L5–S1, followed by ALIF. ACR produced the largest segmental lordosis gains at L2–3 and L3–4, and ALIF did so at L4–5 and L5–S1. Approach choice did not significantly affect lordosis at L1–2. Most LLIF procedures omitted ACR, possibly reflecting surgeon familiarity. ACR significantly improved lordosis at L2–3 and L3–4, but not at L4–5, suggesting that the former levels are the more likely ACR candidates. At L4–5, LLIF and ACR did not differ significantly in lordosis gain; the smaller ACR change may partly reflect the small number treated (n = 4). The authors consider their results consistent with prior reports. Previously published ALIF studies reported segmental lordosis gains from 5.4° to 15°, depending on level. Although ALIF can achieve substantial final lordosis at L5–S1, greater baseline lordosis at that level produces a smaller preoperative-to-postoperative change than at L4–5; the present data showed the same pattern. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Alvi et al. reported mean segmental lordosis gains of 2.1° with static MIS TLIF cages and 5.0° with expandable cages. Hawasli et al. reported corresponding gains of 2.3° and 5.2°. Carlson et al. reported a weighted average gain of 2.1° across cage types and a tendency toward greater postoperative lordosis when cages were placed nearer the anterior vertebral cortex. Other reports have implicated bilateral facetectomies and unilateral pedicle screw instrumentation in greater MIS TLIF lordosis gains. For LLIF without ACR, Xu et al. reported a mean segmental lordosis gain of 5.6° in grade II spondylolisthesis, with complete reduction in 75%. Miscusi et al. reported a mean LLIF lordosis gain of 2.0° and significant mean coronal Cobb angle correction of 11.3°. LLIF with ACR can produce greater segmental lordosis and may supplement or, for selected patients, provide a minimally invasive alternative to posterior osteotomy. Turner et al. reported mean gains of 16.3° with LLIF plus ACR and 5.7° without ACR. In their report, ACR with MIS percutaneous pedicle screw stabilization yielded a 9.9° gain. Another study reported a mean ACR gain of 11.8°, with most procedures at L3–4, as in the present study. The authors emphasize that ACR combined with open pedicle instrumentation and posterior column osteotomies (PCOs) differs from ACR with MIS percutaneous fixation without PCO, the cMIS approach. Reported gains with ACR plus Scoliosis Research Society–Schwab grades 1 or 2 posterior osteotomies were 17.3°–18.7°, but combining PCO with ACR was associated with an almost 7-fold increase in subsidence rates. In the present cMIS cohort, ACR gains of 4°–10° were lower than those in earlier reports. Nevertheless, ACR at cranial lumbar levels can produce more lordosis than TLIF, potentially shortening the construct, and its access corridor is often more favorable than ALIF. Reported ACR complications can be catastrophic, including iliac venous or arterial injury requiring immediate vascular surgical intervention. Reports involving experienced surgeons describe major vascular, visceral, and neurological complications as exceedingly rare (< 1%). The treated level, the relationship of major vessels to the spine, and surgeon familiarity with ACR therefore need individual consideration. Greater segmental lordosis achieved through minimally invasive interbody approaches has been reported to correlate with better patient-reported outcomes. The authors suggest that the underlying mechanism is probably multifactorial, with direct neural decompression through discectomy and indirect decompression of foraminal stenosis as major contributors. How much segmental lordosis gain affects regional LL and PI-LL mismatch depends on approach. Xu et al. reported that LL increased by 52% of the segmental gain with LLIF, compared with 34% with ALIF. For ACR with hyperlordotic cages, a cited study reported LL gains of 81% of segmental gain and PI-LL mismatch improvement of 8.3°. Published MIS TLIF findings put LL change at 45% to 200% of segmental gain, depending on static versus expandable cages. Directly relating segmental gains to LL or PI-LL mismatch remains difficult because of biomechanical effects outside the treated level and changes in global sagittal alignment. The authors note that ALIF correction in cMIS may fall short of the implanted hyperlordotic cage angle because posterior percutaneous instrumentation often does not include facetectomies; they describe a similar effect for LLIF and ACR. Leveque et al. found mean ACR segmental correction equal to 54% of implanted cage lordosis. The present MIS TLIF results were consistent with earlier publications and may represent a reproducible average rather than an upper limit. Some patients, particularly those with collapsed disc spaces or vacuum phenomena, may obtain more TLIF correction, as reported for LLIF. Even so, TLIF produced very little lordosis restoration at L4–5 and L5–S1 in this dataset. An important prerequisite for MIISA is determining whether MIS rather than open correction is appropriate. Early ASD MIS studies reported suboptimal results when SVA exceeded 9.5 cm or required coronal curve correction exceeded 34°. The minimally invasive spinal deformity surgery (MISDEF) algorithm was developed through a comparable Delphi process. Its MISDEF-2 version assigns patients to 1 of 4 classes: Class I and II mild-to-moderate deformities can be managed with MIS decompression and/or interbody fusion; Class III, involving more than 1 adverse predictive sagittal parameter, a rigid spine, or previous instrumentation requiring a short construct, can be treated using cMIS with anterior longitudinal ligament release, expandable cages, mini-open pedicle subtraction osteotomy, or hybrid approaches; Class IV should not receive MIS strategies because open surgery with osteotomies and possible thoracic extension is required. Using MISDEF-2 alongside MIISA may clarify the appropriate overall MIS strategy. In the present study, appropriately selected patients treated with minimally invasive interbodies improved in PI-LL mismatch, coronal Cobb angle, and ODI, indicating that substantial clinical improvement is achievable with less invasive techniques. The authors identify several limitations. Retrospective design and data from a relatively small multicenter group of surgeons introduced hard-to-control variability in collection. One nonsurgeon performed radiographic measurements, preventing calculation of interrater agreement. Cage types—static, expandable, lordotic, or hyperlordotic—were not distinguished despite their influence on attainable lordosis. Approach choices are changing as lateral and ALIF options with greater hyperlordosis become available; graft selection varies, and intraoperative anatomy can prevent use or limit the graft angle. The study intended to provide a general level-specific approach framework and average correction estimates; further research must examine how often lordotic versus 0° cages are used and their outcomes in MIS for ASD. Some patients received different approaches at different levels, making it impossible to attribute changes in pelvic parameters or PI-LL mismatch to one approach alone. Approach groups were unequal, with LLIF used in 70% of cases; this reflects contributing surgeons’ practice but may bias observed mean segmental lordosis. Finally, MIISA does not encompass all ASD MIS decisions. The scoliosis-curve apex, degree and location of neural compression, foraminal osteophytic hooks, vascular anatomy, and previous abdominal or retroperitoneal surgery can strongly affect approach selection and need careful consideration alongside the algorithm.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The study adds to understanding of interbody approach selection for cMIS and hybrid ASD surgery. MIISA is a framework to use together with careful patient selection and assessment of comorbidities, anatomical access restrictions, baseline radiographic findings, and surgical goals. This surgeon group favored lateral approaches over TLIF at L1–4 and reserved ACR for patients requiring the largest segmental lordosis increase. Their preference order at L4–5 was LLIF, TLIF, then ALIF, although TLIF did not demonstrate significant restoration of lordosis. At L5–S1, they generally favored ALIF when more segmental lordosis was wanted and TLIF when preoperative lordosis was adequate. The authors state that larger prospective studies relating outcomes to health-related quality-of-life measures are needed to support these findings.
